## RESULTS

### Schedule Instability and Perceived Social Support

We begin by examining how schedule instability is associated with workers’ perceived social support (Path A in Figure 1). In Table 1, we present estimates from cross-sectional models predicting respondents’ instrumental (M1), emotional (M2), and on-the-job coworker support (M3) as a function of their exposure to schedule instability, including both individual just-in-time scheduling practices and a schedule instability index. We include the scheduling measures in separate models, such that the estimate in each cell is derived from a separate model.

Across all 18 models (3 outcomes × 6 predictors), we consistently find a significant negative association between workers’ exposure to schedule instability and their social support. For example, workers who experienced canceled shifts in the past month experience less instrumental support (b = −0.097, p < 0.001), emotional support (b = −0.438, p < 0.001), and coworker support (b = −0.115, p < 0.001). Taking predicted probabilities, we see that workers who experienced a canceled shift were less likely to report perceived instrumental support (44%) compared with those who did not experience a canceled shift (54%), and those who experienced a canceled shift reported fewer friends and family members they can rely on for advice (4.0) compared with those who did not (4.4).

So far, we have treated each scheduling exposure in isolation. In the last row of Table 1, we estimate the association between an additive scale measure of exposure to unstable and unpredictable scheduling and workers’ perceptions of social support. We find that the schedule instability scale is significantly and negatively associated with perceived instrumental support (b = −0.039, p < 0.001), emotional support (b = −0.198, p < 0.001), and coworker support (b = −0.054, p < 0.001). Examining the marginal effects, for example, we find that workers with no exposure to schedule instability (i.e., a “0” on the schedule instability scale) perceive much higher levels of instrumental support (60%) than those with greatest exposure to all five forms of instability (41%). Similarly, 57% of respondents with no exposure to schedule instability report high levels of coworker support, compared to only 30% of respondents with the most exposure. These models are consistent with the idea that highly unstable and unpredictable schedules undermine workers’ social support of all types. We plot the predicted probabilities for the relationship between the schedule instability scale and social support in Figure 2.

However, it is possible that unobserved, time-constant heterogeneity among workers drives the association between schedule instability and perceived support. For instance, workers with strong interpersonal skills may be more successful in accessing more stable schedules and in maintaining supportive social connections. To assess this possibility, we turn to our panel data, where we leverage respondents’ multiple observations to run individual fixed-effect models. Specifically, we compare 1) how schedule instability predicts support in our cross-sectional data; 2) how schedule instability predicts support cross-sectionally in our pooled panel data (to establish a baseline estimate on a new sample); and 3) how schedule instability predicts support in pooled panel data with individual fixed effects.

We plot the coefficients from each of these models in online supplement, Figure S3. Our results are similar for the cross-sectional analysis of the full sample compared with the smaller panel sample, although the estimates are less precise for the smaller panel sample. When we control for unobserved time-invariant heterogeneity by adding individual fixed effects, we continue to see a negative association between schedule instability and both emotional and coworker support, though the magnitude of the associations are somewhat attenuated. For instrumental support, the association is greatly attenuated in the presence of the individual fixed effects, suggesting either that the association between schedule instability and perceived instrumental support is driven by unobserved heterogeneity or that the processes by which schedule instability shapes instrumental support play out over a longer time horizon.

### The Mediating Role of Perceived Social Support in the Relationship between Schedule Instability and Well-Being

Next, we investigate whether this depletion of social support is one reason why schedules are detrimental for workers’ health, testing the extent to which social support mediates the well-documented relationship between schedule instability and well-being (Schneider and Harknett 2019). This corresponds to path B in our conceptual framework (Figure 1), specifically the pathway between schedule instability and well-being that operates through social support.

We run a series of nested regression models (Table 2), beginning with base models that regress each well-being measure on the schedule instability scale (M1, M5, and M9), then add each social support variable individually to these models. While we report results for all three types of perceived support, it is important to keep in mind that the instrumental support results may be driven by unobserved heterogeneity.

We first see that each social support measure is itself strongly associated with our well-being outcomes, offering further evidence of the direct effect of social support on well-being that has been established in prior work. We also produce estimates of the direct effect of social support on our well-being outcomes without the schedule instability scale in online supplement, Table S1. For example, coworker support is associated with an 11 percentage point decrease in psychological distress (p<0.001), a 13 percentage point increase in higher levels of happiness (p<0.001), and a 14 percentage point increase in good sleep quality (p<0.001). We find a similar pattern of results for both instrumental and emotional support.

We also note that the coefficients for the instability scale are reduced following the addition of each of these social support variables. This suggests that perceived support attenuates the relationship between schedule instability and well-being, specifically psychological distress, happiness, and sleep quality. For example, the coefficient for the effect of the schedule instability scale on happiness is −0.033 (p< 0.001) in the base model, but reduces to −0.028 (p< 0.001) when instrumental support is added, −0.027 (p<0.001) when emotional support is added, and −0.025 (p<0.001) when coworker support is added. This pattern extends to the remaining social support and well-being variables. This attenuation offers evidence of how social support mediates the relationship between schedule instability and well-being.

We next draw on structural equation modeling to decompose the direct and indirect effects to more formally test the hypothesis that social support mediates the relationship between schedule instability and well-being. We find strong evidence of mediation (Table 3). Specifically, the three forms of social support together mediate 24% of the relationship between schedule instability and psychological distress, 41% of the relationship between schedule instability and happiness, and 39% of the relationship between schedule instability and sleep quality.

We further decompose this percentage into the component contributions of each type of social support and find that each type of support plays a mediating role. For example, instrumental support mediates 6% of the relationship between schedule instability and psychological distress, compared to the 11% mediated by emotional support and 7% mediated by coworker support. Of the 41% of the instability-happiness relationship mediated by social support, 10% is mediated by instrumental support, 15% is mediated by emotional support, and 16% is mediated by coworker support. Finally, of the 39% of the instability-sleep relationship mediated by social support, 10% is mediated by instrumental support, 9% is mediated by emotional support, and 19% is mediated by coworker support. In sum, these results suggest that emotional support is the most important mediator for psychological distress and sleep quality and emotional and coworker support are both important mediators when it comes to workers’ happiness. We put more stock in the results for emotional and coworker support given evidence that instrumental support may be subject to bias from unobserved heterogeneity (online supplement, Figure S3).

In online supplement, Table S2, we compare these results to other mediators established by Schneider and Harknett (2019), namely household economic insecurity and work-family conflict. We show that together these three constructs mediate 69% of the relationship between schedule instability and psychological distress, 97% of the relationship between schedule instability and happiness, and 93% of the relationship between schedule instability and sleep quality. Similarly to what Schneider and Harknett (2019) report, work-family conflict is the largest mediator, but social support mediates 7% of the relationship with psychological distress, 18% of the relationship with happiness, and 18% of the relationship with sleep quality.

### The Moderating Role of Perceived Social Support in the Relationship between Schedule Instability and Well-Being

Our analyses to this point offer evidence that unstable and unpredictable schedules deplete workers’ social support (path A), which partly explains the negative relationship between schedule instability and well-being (path B). Next, we consider whether support acts as a buffer (i.e., a moderator) against the negative effects of unstable and unpredictable schedules on well-being (path C in Figure 1).

To test this, we first reproduce prior findings that highlight how schedule instability is significantly negatively associated with well-being (online supplement, Table S3). We then run a series of regression models predicting our three well-being outcomes (psychological distress, happiness, and sleep quality) that include an interaction effect between the schedule instability scale and each social support variable (Table 4). In total, we estimate 9 models (3 outcomes × 3 types of social support).

In the cross-sectional analysis, we find evidence that social support does buffer the negative well-being effects of unstable schedules, but only for certain combinations of support and outcome variables, in line with the matching hypothesis (Jolly et al. 2021; Viswesvaran et al. 1999). Given that our outcomes are most closely tied with respondents’ emotional well-being, it is perhaps unsurprising that we find significant moderating effects of emotional support on both psychological distress (b = −0.004, p <0.001) and happiness (b = 0.003, p <0.001). For example, the interaction effect between schedule instability and emotional support in the psychological distress model is −0.004 (p<0.001), meaning that for each additional unstable scheduling practice that respondents experience, additional emotional support reduces respondents’ psychological distress further.

Figure 3 displays these relationships graphically. As expected given a large literature on the benefits of social support, these figures show that, at all levels of schedule instability, each type of support is associated with better outcomes (e.g., lower distress, more happiness). These figures also show the expected relationship between schedule instability and worse outcomes. Most notably, these figures provide evidence consistent with social support buffering against the harmful effects of precarious work in that the relationship between schedule instability and worse outcomes is muted in the presence of greater amounts of social support.

For example, Figure 3 shows that the elevated distress associated with increasing schedule instability is most pronounced for those lacking in emotional support and is much more muted in the presence of emotional support, consistent with the buffering hypothesis. In particular, going from the most to the least stable schedules is associated with a 30 percentage point increase in distress in the absence of emotional support and just a 12 percentage point increase for those with the most robust emotional support from their social ties. This same pattern appears for emotional support buffering against declines in happiness as schedules become more unstable; declines in happiness are most dramatic for those without any emotional support (declining by 21 percentage points) and are far more muted for those with the most robust emotional support (declining by just 4 percentage points).

Similarly, additional coworker support is associated with improved well-being at higher levels of schedule instability, particularly for happiness (b = 0.012, p<0.05). For example, looking at marginal effects (Figure 3, bottom), among those who lack coworker support, we see a steeper decline in happiness as schedule instability increases, evidence that coworker support buffers against the toll of schedule instability. This suggests that on-the-job social support is an important buffer for the negative effects of schedule instability on well-being.

Instrumental support appears to have little buffering effect compared with emotional or coworker support. The stronger protective effects of emotional and coworker support compared to instrumental support are also in line with the matching hypothesis, specifically that the portion of the relationship between schedule instability and well-being not mediated by social support is driven more by work-life conflict than economic insecurity, as Schneider and Harknett (2019) show in their work. In addition, as shown earlier, the association between schedule instability and instrumental support may be driven by unobserved heterogeneity.

Notably, the buffering pattern reverses for our measure of sleep quality, in that the gap between those with and without social support actually narrows at higher levels of schedule instability, specifically for instrumental support (b = −0.012, p<0.001). These findings suggest that schedules are uniquely bad for sleep, and even high levels of social support are unable to mitigate these negative effects. Furthermore, it is also possible that higher social connectedness (vis-à-vis social support) may create additional time commitments that compete with sleep, particularly if the social support is reciprocal and involves the respondent giving their own time back to their network. In contrast, being socially isolated may mean that, without friends and family to spend time with or take care of, there is more time available to sleep.

## DISCUSSION

Over the last half-century, work in the United States has become increasingly precarious as employers shift market risks to their employees, leading to significant declines in job quality, particularly for workers without a college degree (Hacker 2019; Kalleberg 2009). This includes the use of “just-in-time” scheduling practices, which have far-reaching implications for workers’ well-being and economic security (Lambert et al. 2019; Schneider and Harknett 2019, 2021). More recently, scholarship has also examined a growing trend of social isolation and disconnectedness and how it affects workers’ physical and mental health (Murthy 2017, 2020; Pugh 2024). This research notes that individuals who are more socially isolated and disconnected are likely to have fewer supportive relationships (Cornwell and Waite 2009), but rarely draws a connection to the changing nature of work. Against the backdrop of this rise in precarious working conditions and social disconnectedness, we consider how work both shapes and is shaped by human relationships, specifically workers’ supportive ties to friends, family, and coworkers.

Drawing on novel cross-sectional (N=37,615) and longitudinal (N=5,798 person-wave observations) data from The Shift Project, we show that precarious work creates a “double bind” for workers: exposure to highly unstable and unpredictable schedules creates a need for support to buffer against the negative effects of schedule instability on worker well-being, while at the same time it undermines workers’ perceptions of the social support available to them. As a result, precarious work creates compounding disadvantages: workers who lack social support because of their work schedules are also less able to cope with the negative consequences of those work schedules for their well-being.

Our paper finds that the conditions of precarious work–particularly unstable and unpredictable work schedules–have negative repercussions for supportive social ties. Empirically, we find that service sector workers who are exposed to schedule instability have reduced perceptions of social support, establishing a direct effect of precarious working conditions on workers’ perceptions of social support that was previously unexplored in the extant literature. Strikingly, the consequences of precarious work schedules are not confined to work relationships or particular types of support but are pervasive: having an ever-changing and unpredictable work schedule appears to undermine relationships both at work and outside of work. While prior research has found that schedule instability is negatively associated with well-being (Schneider and Harknett 2019) and social support is positively associated with well-being (Turner and Brown 2010), to our knowledge, ours is the first study to examine the effect of schedule instability on social support.

The negative effect of precarious work schedules on social support has downstream consequences for worker well-being. We show that diminished social support is one of the pathways connecting precarious work and worker well-being, including workers’ psychological distress, happiness, and sleep quality. In doing so, we establish social support as a mediator in the relationship between schedule instability and well-being. Previous research had focused on household economic security and work-life conflict as pathways (Schneider and Harknett 2019) and had not accounted for the role that diminished support plays in explaining the relationship between schedules and well-being.

The availability of support acts as a buffer against the negative effects of precarious scheduling on health and well-being but alignment between the support and the well-being outcome matters. Social support, particularly emotional and coworker support, helps to buffer against the negative effects of schedule instability on workers’ psychological distress and happiness. These findings extend a robust literature on the buffering effects of social support that has been focused more broadly and rarely considers precarious working conditions like schedule instability as a job stressor (Lovejoy et al. 2021). While scholars have previously positioned social support as a buffer against the effects of job stressors on well-being (Cohen and McKay 1984; Jolly et al. 2021; Thoits 1995), no work has specifically considered social support as a potential protective buffer that could mitigate the instability-well-being relationship. We fill this gap by presenting evidence that emotional and coworker support indeed act as buffers against the harmful effects of precarious work schedules on workers’ mental health outcomes but not against diminished sleep quality. We do not find evidence that instrumental support acts as a buffer. This nuanced pattern of findings is in line with the matching hypothesis, which emphasizes the importance of matching job stressor, type of support, and outcome (Cohen and McKay 1984; Jolly et al. 2021; Viswesvaran et al. 1999). Specifically, the stronger buffering effect of workers’ perceived emotional and coworker support (relative to instrumental support) may reflect the match between these types of support and mental health outcomes.

Weaving together these findings, we parse the complex and recursive relationship between schedule instability, perceptions of social support, and worker well-being. We argue that social support is both a mediator and moderator of the relationship between unstable and unpredictable schedules and well-being. As our results highlight, the same precarious working conditions that undermine workers’ perceptions of social support also create a greater need for that support, an unfortunate catch-22 that we call a “double bind.” Indeed, we find evidence that precarious work generally, and schedule instability specifically, reduces workers’ assessments of the social support available to them, including different forms (i.e., emotional vs. instrumental) and different sources (e.g., friends, family, coworkers). This lack of social support helps explain the negative effects of schedule instability on worker well-being. However, at the same time, workers exposed to high levels of schedule instability are those most in need of this social support and potentially stand to gain the most from its buffering effect. In this way, these service sector workers are “doubly disadvantaged” (Jack 2019).

In interpreting our findings, there are some limitations that should be kept in mind. Although we highlight how schedule instability is strongly associated with reduced perceptions of social support, we are unable to determine the specific mechanism governing this relationship, although we point to several potential mechanisms based on prior literature (e.g., disrupting the formation and maintenance of network ties, draining networks through mobilization). Future work, particularly qualitative work, would do well to unpack these mechanisms. Given the focus of the Shift Project, our sample and the conclusions of this paper are necessarily limited to service sector workers in the U.S., but while schedule instability is rampant in the service sector, many other workers across different industries grapple with schedule instability, such as healthcare workers (Clawson and Gerstel 2014), software engineers (O’Carroll 2015), and truck drivers (Snyder 2016). Lastly, as noted, The Shift Project data is a non-probability sample, which introduces potential concerns around selection bias based on observed and unobserved characteristics. However, we have conducted several tests to assuage these concerns using the Facebook recruitment platform and The Shift Project panel data, such as using sample weights and individual fixed effects.

Our work has direct implications for policymaking at the local, state, and federal levels. Sociologists have long written about how these private safety nets are critical for individuals and families to cope with the deleterious effects of poverty, particularly in light of the retrenchment of the U.S. public safety net (Edin and Lein 1997, 1998; Edin and Shaefer 2015; Nelson 2000; Stack 2003). However, our work reveals an inherent limitation of a reliance on private safety nets. The “double bind” we describe in this paper means that workers’ private safety nets are unable to effectively buffer against the consequences of precarious work, as those same conditions that produce need also reduce the support workers have available to them to cope with that need.

Next, although some firms voluntarily opt to provide more stable and predictable schedules in an approach that is often described as taking the “high road” (Osterman 2018), some states, counties, and cities have instead opted to “raise the floor” by passing legislation that mandates some minimum level of schedule predictability and advanced notice (Wolfe, Jones, and Cooper 2018). While these secure scheduling laws have demonstrable effects both on workers’ schedule stability and their well-being, our findings suggest that these laws may also have broader implications for workers’ access to social support, which may partly explain the positive effects of this legislation on worker well-being. Finally, both social scientists (Parigi and Henson 2014; Pugh 2024) and public health leaders (Murthy 2017, 2020) have called attention to the rise in social isolation and disconnectedness that has left many individuals without supportive relationships upon which they can rely in times of need. Our research suggests that precarious work may be one contributing factor to this disconnectedness, potentially by reducing opportunities to cultivate and maintain ties at and outside of work or by creating conditions that necessitate the repeated mobilization of these supportive ties, such as through heightened experiences of material hardship (Schneider and Harknett 2021). Public and private initiatives that foster connection and promote meaningful relationships, then, may help to mitigate the consequences of precarious working conditions on individuals’ social support networks and, in turn, on workers’ well-being.

This paper also has important takeaways for a broader sociological audience. We emphasize the need to take seriously the ways that work shapes and is shaped by human relationships, both at work and in workers’ personal lives. Too often, scholarship focuses primarily on one of these domains, as research on low-wage work tends to focus on the conditions of and relationships at work, while the research on coping mechanisms of individuals and families in poverty tend to consider work only insofar as it produces the conditions of poverty. We argue that scholars must broaden their lens and consider the multi-faceted and interdependent nature of these individuals’ work and personal lives. Furthermore, the social world is complex and constructs like social support rarely operate in a single or uniform fashion, but empirical research tends to examine social support either as a moderator or a mediator. In contrast, we demonstrate that social support plays multiple roles in the relationship between schedule instability and well-being, highlighting the importance of more nuanced and comprehensive conceptualizations of empirical relationships. Finally, there is a long-standing tradition in sociology of analyzing how changing working conditions affect workers, from the focus of early social theorists like Marx and Durkheim on rising industrialization to contemporary scholarship on precarious work. In documenting the relationship between schedule instability, social support, and well-being, we offer further evidence of the insidious and far-reaching effects of poor job quality for workers.

# Temporal Autonomy: Schedule Instability as a Threat to Perceived Dignity in the U.S. Service Sector

**Authors:** Tyler Woods

**Affiliations:** Harvard Kennedy School, USA

## Abstract

The dignity of workers has long been a central concern of social scientists, with existing research documenting the variety of job conditions that threaten worker dignity. However, the literature on dignity at work has important limitations, including an overwhelming focus on older models of work (e.g., manufacturing), to the exclusion of the job conditions that are pervasive in the contemporary low-wage labor market, such as unstable and unpredictable schedules. Drawing on individual-level survey data on 17,791 service sector workers from the Shift Project, I test the association between schedule instability and perceived worker dignity, which I operationalize as perceived respect and recognition from supervisors, as well as how this varies by gender. Overall, I find that workers’ schedule instability is significantly and negatively associated with perceived worker dignity. This holds for five just-in-time scheduling practices and for a schedule instability index that captures the cumulative effect of exposure to unstable scheduling. I also document gender differences in the association between schedule instability and perceived worker dignity. Specifically, I show that the consequences of schedule instability for perceptions of supervisor respect are more negative for women than men, which is, in part, driven by work-family conflict.

The dignity of workers has long been a central concern of social scientists across disciplines, motivating the work of management scholars (Lucas et al. 2017), organizational psychologists (Eisenberger, Shanock, and Wen 2020), and sociologists of work and occupations (Hodson 2001; Hodson and Roscigno 2004; Reich and Bearman 2018. Although a concrete definition has proven elusive, scholars have elucidated dignity as a multidimensional concept (Bolton and Wibberley 2007) encompassing respect and recognition at work (Hodson 2001; Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021). Above and beyond the moral imperative to treat workers fairly as full people worthy of respect (Sayer 2007), promoting dignity at work has positive effects on workers’ psychological well-being (Crowley 2012; Hodson 2001) and can complement organizational success (Crowley 2016; Hodson and Roscigno 2004; Lucas et al. 2017; Ton 2014).

What, then, are the conditions under which workers are deprived of dignity at work? A robust body of empirical research establishes that various job conditions at the organizational, interpersonal, and individual levels can threaten dignity at work (Gibson et al. 2023). At the organizational level, scholars point to job conditions that reduce autonomy and lead to alienation and disaffection, such as high levels of employee control and surveillance (Crowley 2012; Gibson et al. 2023; Laaser and Bolton 2022; Wheatley 2017). At the interpersonal level, work environments with abusive supervision and bullying from coworkers and supervisors likewise may threaten workers’ dignity (Einarsen, Hoel, and Cooper 2002; Hodson, Roscigno, and Lopez 2006; Nielsen and Einarsen 2012; Tepper 2007). At the individual level, workers with particular social identities or working in stigmatized jobs and tasks may experience less respect and recognition at work (Brooks 2019; Gibson et al. 2023; Lamont 2000, Lamont et al. 2016; Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021).

However, many of these studies, particularly the large number that rely on the corpus of existing workplace ethnographies (see Hodson and Roscigno 2004), examine older forms of work arrangements, such as manufacturing and factory work. With few exceptions (e.g., Dube, Naidu, and Reich 2022; Karlsson 2012; Korczynski and Evans 2013; Leidner 1993; Reich and Bearman 2018), scholarship on dignity at work has not focused on newer and more widespread models of work, such as the service sector. This represents a notable gap, given the sharp rise in the proportion of the U.S. work-force in the service sector over the last several decades (Barnes, Bauer, and Edelberg 2022). Service sector jobs exemplify the rising precarity of work (Kalleberg 2011), where the increasing dominance of neoliberalism and shareholder value strategies within firms (Crowley 2016; Fligstein and Goldstein 2022; Fligstein and Shin 2007), declining worker power (Rosenfeld 2014), and an intense focus on cost-cutting to increase profits (Cappelli et al. 1997; Hirsch and De Soucey 2006) has led to substantial declines in job quality (e.g., low and stagnant wages, reduced fringe benefits).

The lack of scholarship on dignity in the service sector means that we know relatively little about how precarious job conditions that are prevalent in the service sector are associated with workers’ dignity. More specifically, little work has examined the relationship between worker dignity and workers’ control over their time, a key aspect of job quality today for low-wage workers (Gerstel and Clawson 2018; Lambert, Haley-Lock, and Henly 2012; Schneider and Harknett 2019). In contrast to earlier eras, where a 9-to-5, Monday through Friday schedule was the dominant model, many workers today contend with nonstandard and unpredictable schedules (Gerstel and Clawson 2018; Presser 2005). Schedule instability, from on-call shifts to last-minute timing changes and cancellations, is both widespread and highly consequential for worker well-being (Lambert 2008; Lambert, Henly, and Kim 2019; Schneider and Harknett 2019, 2021).

Missing from the extant literature, though, is a conceptualization and empirical investigation of schedule instability as a threat to dignity, insofar as control over one’s work schedule represents a form of temporal autonomy. The service sector is a strategic site to investigate this question, as service sector jobs are rife with unstable and unpredictable work schedules (Lambert 2008; Schneider and Harknett 2019), and, thus, workers may suffer from a lack of dignity related to their control over work time. This is a significant opportunity to further our understanding of how job conditions shape worker dignity, in a particularly salient manifestation of modern-day job quality: work schedules.

Prior research suggests that work schedules may have notable implications for worker dignity, specifically workers’ perceptions of respect and recognition (Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021). As a result of intense neoliberal pressures to maximize short-term profit by reducing labor costs (Crowley 2016; Fligstein and Goldstein 2022; Fligstein and Shin 2007), many service sector employers now use “just-in-time” scheduling practices to match employee staffing with consumer demand, giving hourly workers little advanced notice of their schedules or altering schedules last minute to pass on market risks (Lambert 2008; Lambert, Haley-Lock, and Henly 2012). This schedule instability creates chaos at work (Hodson, Roscigno, and Lopez 2006; Juravich 1985) that also permeates workers’ personal lives, from material hardship to parental and marital strain to negative health effects (Luhr, Schneider, and Harknett 2022; Presser 2000; Schneider and Harknett 2019, 2021). Workers’ temporal autonomy may be associated with perceptions of respect and recognition from supervisors in particular, given the extent to which frontline managers exert control over individual workers’ schedules (Reich and Bearman 2018; Wheatley 2017; Wood 2020). Furthermore, prior work on relational managerial citizenship behavior (e.g., Hodson 2002b; Rubin and Brody 2011), a concept closely linked to dignity that emphasizes managers’ behaviors that conform to workplace norms, points to the importance of supervisory respect and recognition for workers, but we know little about how these might be associated with schedule instability. To my knowledge, this study is among the first to examine the implications of unstable and unpredictable schedules on dignity-related outcomes such as respect and recognition.

Organizations and organizational processes are not gender neutral (Acker 1990), so there is also reason to suspect that the dignity-related consequences of just-in-time scheduling practices may vary by gender. Recent sociological scholarship documents variation in how gender discrimination and sexual harassment affect men’s and women’s experiences of respect and recognition, pointing to the gendered nature of dignity at work and concluding that “women experience less dignity at work than do men” (Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021:562). Prior research also identifies an association between schedule instability and work-family conflict for women (Luhr, Schneider, and Harknett 2022; Lyness et al. 2012), in line with other research highlighting the uneven distribution of work-family challenges for men and women (Collins 2019; Kelly, Moen, and Tranby 2011). However, no research to date has examined whether gender may moderate the association between schedule instability and workers’ perceptions of dignity.

In this study, I address these key empirical and theoretical gaps, building upon prior literatures on dignity, managerial citizenship behavior, and precarious work to conceptualize unstable schedules as a threat to dignity at work, manifest in the worker-supervisor relationship, and one that may be experienced differently by men and women. Specifically, I examine whether schedule instability is associated with two measures of perceived dignity: perceptions of respect and perceptions of recognition from supervisors among U.S. service sector workers. I consider five individual just-in-time scheduling practices (canceled shifts; changes in timing; working a “clopening” shift, that is, working an opening shift immediately following a closing shift; being on-call; and receiving less than two weeks of notice for schedules), as well as a schedule instability scale that captures the cumulative exposure to unstable schedules. I also test whether gender moderates the relationship between schedule instability and perceived respect and recognition from supervisors. To do this, I draw on novel individual-level survey data from 17,791 service sector workers collected between spring 2023 and spring 2024. These data come from the Shift Project, which, since 2016, has surveyed hourly workers at over 200 large firms in the service sector in the United States, using advertisements on Facebook to sample and recruit respondents (Schneider and Harknett 2022). The Shift Project captures uniquely detailed measures of exposure to just-in-time scheduling practices, and, in recent survey waves, fielded a module on workers’ experiences of dignity in the workplace. Existing data sources rarely contain information on both dignity-related outcomes and exposure to schedule instability, so survey data from the Shift Project are unique in facilitating the study of this relationship, addressing a key gap in the literature.

Overall, I find that workers’ exposure to schedule instability is significantly and negatively associated with feelings of respect and recognition from supervisors. This holds for all five just-in-time scheduling practices and for a schedule instability index that captures cumulative exposure. I also document notable gender differences in the effect of schedule instability on supervisor respect. Specifically, I find that the consequences of schedule instability for perceptions of respect from supervisors are more negative for women than men. Decomposition analyses suggest that the moderating effect of gender may be partly explained by work-family conflict.

## BACKGROUND: DIGNITY

### Defining and Operationalizing Dignity

Scholarly interest in dignity at work dates to the foundations of modern social science. Indeed, early social theorists were fundamentally concerned with the dignity of workers in the context of changing social and institutional norms (Hodson 2001). As Sharon Bolton (2007) notes, the founding figures of sociology each conceptualized rising industrialization as a potential threat to workers’ dignity. Building on these theoretical underpinnings, contemporary scholars of work and organizational behavior have made strides in defining dignity and identifying, both theoretically and empirically, the factors that threaten or promote dignity. The sociologist Randy Hodson (2001:3), in his pioneering book Dignity at Work, defines dignity as “the ability to establish a sense of self-worth and self-respect and to appreciate the respect of others,” while Gibson et al. (2023:230) define dignity at work as “the inherent and earned worth, value, and esteem experienced by individuals at work in the absence of disaffection, exclusion, and expendability, and in the presence of connectedness, respect, and meaningfulness.”

Scholars have documented myriad factors that threaten dignity at work. In secondary qualitative analysis of over 140 workplace organizational ethnographies, Hodson (2001) identifies four primary threats to dignity (mismanagement and abuse, overwork, contradictions of employee involvement, and a lack of autonomy), as well as four pathways to safeguarding dignity (resistance, citizenship, autonomous meaning systems, and coworker relations). Importantly, Hodson (2001) emphasizes that dignity is fundamentally relational, in that employers can deny dignity and employees can work to preserve it. Research has explored each of these factors and more, identifying negative consequences for worker dignity from abusive supervision and bullying (Roscigno, Lopez, and Hodson 2009; Tepper 2007); low pay (Berg and Frost 2006); social status and cultural identity (Lamont 2000); organizational context and management behavior (Hodson 2002a; Hodson, Roscigno, and Lopez 2006; Roscigno, Lopez, and Hodson 2009); and employee control and a lack of autonomy (Chamberlain and Hodson 2010; Crowley 2012; Laaser and Bolton 2022). For example, Hodson (2002a) finds that management leadership, and particularly respect for workers’ rights, are significant predictors of meaning and dignity at work, while Roscigno, Lopez, and Hodson (2009) highlight how chaotic and disorganized organizations can create environments that facilitate supervisory bullying and threaten dignity. However, scholars define dignity in diverse ways (Gibson et al. 2023; Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021), which is both a strength (given that the concept can be applied to many research areas) and a challenge (given the lack of comparability across studies).

Recent work has established that dignity is a multidimensional concept derived from relational interactional processes, with two critical dimensions being respect and recognition (Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021). Gibson et al. (2023) and Lucas et al. (2017) distinguish between inherent dignity, which involves treating workers as more than simply a means to an end, and earned dignity, which concerns the fair distribution of rewards and opportunity within the workplace; the former concerns respect, while the latter concerns recognition (Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021). Using the framework developed by Gibson et al. (2023), I am primarily interested in policies and practices at the organizational and interpersonal levels that shape dignity, manifest in feeling respected and valued (i.e., recognized). A robust literature has identified respect and recognition as critical elements of worker dignity (Hodson 2002a; Laaser and Bolton 2022; Lamont 2000; Lamont et al. 2016; Reich and Bearman 2018), with recognition primarily being operationalized as a function of being treated fairly (Dube, Naidu, and Reich 2022; Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021).

Relatedly, scholars have expanded Hodson’s focus on mismanagement as a threat to dignity into the concept of managerial citizenship behavior (Crowley 2016; Hodson 1999, 2002b; Rubin and Brody 2011). Hodson (2002b:65) defines managerial citizenship as “behavior that conforms to prevailing norms for organizational leadership and for respecting workers’ rights.” Managerial citizenship involves two primary domains: 1) relational behaviors that demonstrate respect for employees and 2) operational competence (Crowley 2016; Hodson 2002b; Rubin and Brody 2011), though scholars have built on these foundations to add ethical and family-supportive behaviors (Rubin and Brody 2011). Importantly, Rubin and Brody (2011) operationalization of relational managerial citizenship behavior has close parallels to Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin (2021) definition of dignity, as it includes measures of supervisory respect and recognition.

In this study, I draw on Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin (2021) operationalization of the dignity construct as a function of respect and recognition. And, building on prior work on managerial citizenship behavior that points to the importance of supervisory behavior for workers’ experiences of dignity (Brody, Rubin, and Maume 2014; Crowley 2016; Hodson 1999, 2002b; Rubin and Brody 2011), I focus specifically on respect and recognition from workers’ supervisors.

### Dignity in the Service Sector

One limitation of existing scholarship on dignity at work is its occupational focus. A significant number of articles and books, particularly in sociology, rely on the Workplace Ethnography Project (WEP) (Hodson 2004), which content coded over 200 organizational ethnographies, drawing out salient themes related to dignity at work. This project has served as the foundation for many studies (e.g., Crowley 2012; Hodson 2001; Hodson and Roscigno 2004; Hodson, Roscigno, and Lopez 2006; Roscigno, Lopez, and Hodson 2009) and has significantly advanced our understanding of the drivers and consequences of dignity at work. Because of the substantive foci of the ethnographies on which it relies, the WEP and the resulting publications offer analyses of dignity that span industrial, professional, managerial, and blue-collar operations. However, given the time horizon in which these books were published, much of this research privileges older models of work, such as manufacturing, at the expense of in-depth analyses of newer work arrangements.

In particular, scholarship rarely centers the dignity of workers in the service sector, a fast-growing and precarious segment of the U.S. labor market (Kalleberg 2011; Osterman and Shulman 2011). Over the last several decades, the United States has shifted from a goods-producing to a services-producing economy, and scholars have suggested that low-wage service sector jobs have replaced many higher-paying manufacturing jobs (Kalleberg 2011). For example, manufacturing employment fell by 34 percent between 1979 and 2019 (Harris 2020), while, over the same period, employment in service-providing industries increased by over 100 percent (Barnes, Bauer, and Edelberg 2022).

The origins of the increasingly precarious nature of low-wage work in the United States are complex, resulting from a variety of social, political, and economic forces. One key factor is the rise of shareholder value strategies in firms, whereby managers are pressured by financially-oriented investors to increase the return on firm assets for their shareholders and decrease investments in their workers (Fligstein and Shin 2007; Lazonick and O’Sullivan 2000). Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, a small number of firms controlled the U.S. economy, generating large revenues and investing those profits in their physical capital and human resources. However, struggling with slow economic growth and rising inflation (i.e., “stagflation”) in the early 1980s, managers at large firms began to face extreme pressure from financial investors to increase profits (Fligstein and Shin 2007). Economic sociologists such as Neil Fligstein (2001) describe this as the emergence of the “shareholder value conception of the firm,” whereby it is the role of top managers to make sure the firm returns the highest profits possible for their shareholders, at the expense of other stakeholders, such as workers. The increasing focus of businesses on maximizing shareholder value occurred concurrently with, and in many cases was directly influenced by, a sociopolitical context of neoliberalism (Crowley 2016), declining unionization and worker power within firms (Rosenfeld 2014), and increased foreign competition that prompted cost-cutting pressures for U.S. firms (Fligstein and Goldstein 2022; Lin 2016), leading to significant reductions in labor costs. These forces collectively resulted in a precarious labor market with declining job quality, manifest in low and stagnant wages, increased nonstandard work arrangements, decreased job security, fewer fringe benefits, and unstable and unpredictable work schedules (Autor and Dorn 2013; Kalleberg 2011; Lambert 2008).

Despite these significant changes to the contemporary labor market, scholarship on dignity does not necessarily reflect the modern experience of precarious work, particularly given how different service sector work is from the manufacturing and professional jobs often discussed in the classic literature on dignity. There are several notable exceptions to this focus, such as Leidner (1993) seminal study of McDonald’s workers. She finds that efforts to standardize and routinize work in the service sector, whereby firms regulate how workers appear and interact with customers and each other using “scripts,” have negative consequences for worker dignity. Hodson, Roscigno, and Lopez (2006) show that low-status service work and job insecurity are associated with relational powerlessness, which can give rise to bullying at work and threaten worker dignity. In more recent research, Reich and Bearman (2018) examine the experiences of Walmart workers, showing that workers desire recognition from their coworkers as valued community members, while customer interactions and organizational practices like “Walmartism” (i.e., managers’ use of surveillance technology to monitor performance) lead workers to feel disrespected. Other research has examined dignity in the context of modern work more broadly, such as Karlsson (2012) study of organizational misbehavior and Laaser and Ch Karlsson (2023) study of meaningful work. However, this research rarely investigates how elements specific to service work are associated with dignity, particularly workers’ control over time vis-à-vis their work schedules.

### Dignity and Schedule Instability in the Service Sector

The growth of precarious work in the service sector has had a number of implications for workers’ job quality, including low and stagnant wages, declines in fringe benefits, and increased nonstandard work arrangements (Kalleberg 2011). One notable feature of this rising precarity is the decline in workers’ control over their own time, manifest in nonstandard, unstable, and unpredictable schedules (Gerstel and Clawson 2018). Indeed, schedule instability in the service sector is both widespread and consequential (Lambert 2008; Schneider and Harknett 2019), with negative effects on workers’ physical and mental health, economic security, and work-family conflict (Lambert, Haley-Lock, and Henly 2012; Lambert, Henly, and Kim 2019; Schneider and Harknett 2019, 2021). Workers experience unstable and unpredictable schedules primarily because firms pass on market risks to their employees (Hacker 2019), using “just-in-time” scheduling practices (e.g., on-call shifts, last-minute changes to timing) to match staffing to demand (Lambert 2008). These scheduling practices are fundamentally rooted in the same forces that contributed to the growing precarity of work more broadly, including neoliberal policies that sapped worker power within firms and prioritized profit.

To date, however, schedule instability has been undertheorized in sociology as a potential detractor of dignity at work, insofar as workers’ control over their time (Gerstel and Clawson 2018) represents a form of autonomy (Hodson 2001; Wheatley 2017), particularly temporal autonomy. Instead, the literatures on precarious work and dignity have mostly been siloed from one another. While extant scholarship has examined how work time shapes dignity vis-à-vis overwork (Hodson 2001), the (un) predictability of work schedules has rarely been part of this conversation. Wheatley (2017) includes schedule control as one element of autonomy in his analysis of how autonomy shapes subjective well-being, finding that schedule control is positively associated with well-being and job satisfaction. However, this study does not examine how schedule control shapes worker dignity, operationalized as respect and recognition. Other relevant research has shown how job insecurity more broadly (rather than schedule instability specifically) has notable implications for workers’ orientation toward work and work effort (Crowley, Payne, and Kennedy 2020) and experiences of bullying (Hodson, Roscigno, and Lopez 2006; Roscigno, Lopez, and Hodson 2009). For example, Roscigno and colleagues (2009) note that the sort of job insecurity that characterizes low-wage, low-status, precarious work reduces worker power relative to their bosses, a dynamic clearly present in the issue of schedule control and stability.

Respect and recognition from workers’ supervisors may be an important site of investigation for how schedule instability is associated with worker dignity. Managerial practice can significantly impact workers’ experience of work-life balance (McCarthy, Darcy, and Grady 2010) and workplace dignity (Bolton and Wibberley 2007). Bolton and Houlihan (2010) note that frontline service sector managers are mediators of divergent interests, attempting to balance the maximization of profits for the firm with the needs of their employees. Similarly, Vermeerbergen, McDermott, and Benders (2021) emphasize that managers must balance the interests of various stakeholders, as their decisions on issues such as work design have a direct impact on workers. This is especially evident in managers’ control over workers’ schedules (McCallum 2020; Reich and Bearman 2018; Wood 2020). As Wood (2020) makes clear, flexible scheduling is a reflection of managerial power and a form of workplace control, what he terms “flexible despotism,” and workers actively attempt to gain favor with their managers to receive better schedules (i.e., “scheduling gifts”).

Scholarship on managerial citizenship behaviors also points to the important role of supervisors for workers’ well-being and dignity, as mismanagement represents one of the key threats to dignity identified by Hodson (2001). For example, Hodson (2002b) shows that managerial citizenship behaviors can reduce conflict between managers and workers and among coworkers, while Rubin and Brody (2011) document strong positive effects of managerial citizenship behaviors, including workers’ perceptions of supervisor respect and recognition, on workers’ organizational commitment, job satisfaction, and mental health. However, research has not tested whether workers’ experiences of schedule instability shape their perceptions of supervisor respect and recognition.

Because of supervisors’ control over employees’ schedules, workers are likely to attribute their poor schedules to their supervisors, meaning we would expect the dignity-related consequences of schedule instability to manifest in the worker-supervisor relationship. And, even if managerial discretion is limited and managers themselves are implementing company-wide policies and practices on scheduling, workers still view their supervisors as a proxy for the organization as a whole (Eisenberger et al. 2002; Haar, De Fluiter, and Brougham 2016; Havard, Rorive, and Sobczak 2009). As a result, I argue that workers experience control over their own time, or a lack thereof, as a reflection of respect and recognition from their supervisors. Workers with unpredictable schedules may feel like their employers treat them as a cost to be managed rather than as people with personal lives affected by their work schedules (Alvarez et al. 2020; Hodson 2002a), such that schedule instability may be associated with workers feeling like their supervisor does not respect them. Furthermore, workers may feel that they are unfairly given bad schedules compared to their coworkers (Wood 2020), leading to feelings that their supervisor does not recognize them.

### Gender, Dignity, and Schedule Instability

Dignity at work may be experienced differently based on gender, given the normative and structural constraints on women within organizations that create conflict between work and social roles (Acker 1990). For example, the dignity-related consequences of schedule instability may not be experienced in the same way by men and women in the service sector, although the direction of this moderating relationship is unclear, given the mixed findings in the extant literature. On the one hand, it is possible that women experience less dignity when they experience just-in-time scheduling practices because of their implications for work-life conflict (Hill et al. 2013), particularly given women’s role in family life, from childrearing (Bianchi 2000) to cognitive labor (Daminger 2019). Luhr, Schneider, and Harknett (2022), for example, demonstrate how unpredictable and unstable schedules are positively associated with greater work-life conflict. The consequences of working non-standard schedules also differ for men and women, in part because of the greater complexity of childcare (Presser 2005). Scholars have shown that job and schedule control are significantly associated with work-family conflict for women (Hwang and Ramadoss 2017; Lyness et al. 2012). For example, Lyness et al. (2012) show that a lack of schedule control is associated with increased work-family conflict, but only for women.

Beyond work schedules, women more often encounter coercive bundles of control (e.g., direct supervision) that erode the foundations of dignity at work and a meaningful work experience (Crowley 2013), while female managers experience fewer benefits of managerial citizenship behaviors than do male managers (Brody, Rubin, and Maume 2014). Furthermore, recent evidence suggests that women experience less dignity at work, as measured by respect and recognition, as a result of gender discrimination and sexual harassment, despite reporting similar levels of job satisfaction (Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021). Schedule instability may likewise contribute to the gendered nature of dignity at work and the gender respect gap identified by Roscigno and colleagues.

On the other hand, women may not report diminished dignity from schedule instability because of the so-called “female paradox,” whereby women appraise their job more positively than men do, despite experiencing substantially greater labor market inequalities (Buchanan 2005; Zou 2015). There are a number of potential explanations for this, including the theory of same-gender referents (i.e., women compare themselves to other women) and rewards expectations theory (i.e., how gender patterns cultural beliefs regarding men’s competence and worthiness) (see Auspurg, Hinz, and Sauer 2017). Along similar lines, Hodson (2002a) finds that men and women respond similarly to the effect of workplace conditions on meaning and satisfaction at work, suggesting that there may be little difference in how schedule instability is associated with men’s and women’s experiences of respect and recognition. Furthermore, women have long faced extreme devaluation at work (Cohen and Huffman 2003; England 1992), evident, for example, in the well-documented gender wage gap (Blau and Kahn 2017). In the context of such devaluation, schedule instability may have a relatively weak impact on women’s assessments of respect and recognition from their supervisors even beyond these other factors.

## DATA AND METHODS

### The Shift Project Data

I use novel survey data from the Shift Project, which has collected data on nearly 200,000 frontline workers across over 200 major service sector firms. These firms span industries such as retail, pharmacy, grocery, hardware, electronics, fast food, hospitality, and more. The Shift Project initially focused primarily on unstable and unpredictable work schedules in the service sector, but has expanded over the years as a broader study of the contours and consequences of precarious work in the service sector, including trends in job conditions and their implications for workers’ health and well-being. Since 2017, the project has conducted sixteen bi-annual rounds of cross-sectional data collection, with the latest in spring 2024, as well as six rounds of longitudinal data collection. In this study, my analysis focuses on data from the fourteenth (spring 2023), fifteenth (fall 2023), and sixteenth (spring 2024) cross-sections (N=17,791).

The Shift Project uses targeted advertisements on Facebook and Instagram to reach workers in prominent U.S. service sector employers (Schneider and Harknett 2022). The project leverages detailed information in users’ profiles, including their employer, available in the Facebook advertising platform. This enables precise targeting of service sector workers at specific firms, meaning that Facebook serves as both a quasi-sampling frame and recruitment device. Paid advertisements appear in users’ newsfeeds, inviting them to take a brief survey and offering a chance to win a $500 gift card. Upon clicking, users are redirected to Qualtrics for an online survey.

Given that recruitment occurs through social media platforms, the Shift Project’s sample is not a probability sample, raising potential concerns about non-coverage and selection bias. Although not reaching the entire target population is possible, both the Facebook and Instagram platforms boast high user engagement. Around 70 percent of working-age individuals have profiles (Auxier and Anderson 2021), reducing concerns around non-coverage. Additionally, selection bias based on observed and unobserved characteristics may exist. In supplementary analyses, I apply post-stratification weights based on demographic characteristics to align my sample with similar industry and occupation groups in the American Community Survey (ACS), and results are fully robust to this specification. Furthermore, prior research suggests that the Shift Project sample aligns well with gold-standard probability samples, such as the Current Population Survey (CPS) and the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY97) (Schneider and Harknett 2022).

The core Shift Project survey covers various topics, including respondent demographics, employment conditions, economic status, benefits receipt, and health and well-being. Its strengths include its focus on frontline workers, comprehensive job quality measures, employer-employee linkage for estimating employer fixed-effects models, and survey adaptability. The fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth rounds of the Shift Project survey (conducted in spring 2023, fall 2023, and spring 2024, respectively) incorporated detailed measures of dignity in the workplace, covering topics such as respect, recognition, and bullying. My analysis is the first to leverage these rich data with uniquely detailed information on both schedule instability and worker dignity, comprising 17,791 workers with complete information on all covariates.

### Key Variables

#### Dignity.

To operationalize dignity, I employ two measures: perceived supervisor respect and perceived fair treatment from supervisors.

#### Perceived supervisor respect.

In order to capture the “respect” dimension of dignity, I draw on a measure of workers’ self-rated perceptions of respect in the workplace. The Shift Project asked workers about their experiences of respect at work from three sources: “How often do you feel respected by…” 1) “your customers?”; 2) “your coworkers?”; and 3) “your supervisor?”. The response options include “Never,” “Rarely,” “Sometimes,” “Often,” and “Always.” I assign each response option a value ranging from 0 (“Never”) to 5 (“Always”). I then create a dichotomous variable, where I collapse “Never,” “Rarely,” and “Sometimes” into “Low Frequency” (0) and “Often” and “Always” into “High Frequency” (1). I use this dichotomous measure primarily for interpretability, but I employ a continuous version of this variable (0–5) in supplementary analyses and results are similar. I focus specifically on respect from supervisors, building on prior work on respect as a key aspect of dignity (Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin 2021) and managerial citizenship behavior (Hodson 1999, 2002b; Rubin and Brody 2011).

#### Perceived recognition.

Recent scholarship has made strides in defining recognition, particularly cultural sociologists such as Michèle Lamont (Lamont 2023), who defines recognition gaps as “disparities in worth and cultural membership between groups” (Lamont 2018:421). Scholars of work and occupations have conceptualized recognition somewhat differently, focusing instead on the extent to which distributional processes within workplaces are equitable and just (Bolton 2007; Laaser and Ch Karlsson 2022; Sayer 2007), building on sociological literature on justice evaluations (Alwin 1987; Arts and van der Veen 1992; Auspurg, Hinz, and Sauer 2017; Jasso 1980; Liebig and Sauer 2016). In this approach, to be “recognized” is to be treated fairly at work. However, while they may foreground different aspects of recognition, these two approaches are more similar than they may seem. For example, Lamont (2018) argues that cultural groups’ claims for recognition include protesting unfair treatment, insofar as being treated unfairly is indicative of being considered less worthy. To capture the recognition dimension of dignity, I follow Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin (2021) in drawing on a measure of respondents’ perceptions of fair treatment from their supervisor, which is also in line with prior work on managerial citizenship behaviors (Hodson 1999, 2002b; Rubin and Brody 2011). By using a measure of recognition similar to previous scholarship on dignity at work, this paper is both in conversation with and more comparable to that research.

The Shift Project asked workers about whether they believe they are treated fairly: “At [EMPLOYER NAME], my immediate supervisor treats me fairly.” The response options included “Always True,” “Often True,” “Sometimes True,” and “Never True.” I assign each response option a value ranging from 0 (“Never True”) to 3 (“Always True”), then dichotomize this into “Low Frequency” (Never or Sometimes) and “High Frequency” (Often or Always).

#### Schedule instability.

I draw upon two sets of measures of workers’ exposure to schedule instability. To capture the range of experiences of schedule instability, I examine five dichotomous measures of unstable scheduling practices (canceled shift, changed timing, “clopenings,” on-call shifts, and less than two weeks of notice). Respondents were asked whether they had experienced any of these practices over the past month (yes or no). These five variables are included as dichotomous measures (0/1). Furthermore, I create an index of the number of unstable scheduling practices that a worker experiences, ranging from 0 to 5, capturing cumulative exposure to schedule instability.

#### Gender.

The Shift Project captures workers’ demographic characteristics, including self-reported measures of gender. Gender is coded as a dichotomous variable (Male and Female), with the very small number of transgender and non-binary respondents excluded from the sample for this analysis.

#### Work-family conflict.

I follow Luhr, Schneider, and Harknett (2022) by employing a work-family conflict scale consisting of three items: “It is easy to get time off when I need it”; “It is difficult to deal with family or personal matters during working hours”; and “In my work schedule, I have enough flexibility to handle family needs.” The response options for the first measure (“get time off”) included “Strongly Agree,” “Agree,” “Disagree,” and “Strongly Disagree.” I collapse “Strongly Agree” and “Agree” into “0” and “Strongly Disagree and Disagree” into “1.” The other two measures have response options that include “Always True,” “Often True,” “Sometimes True,” and “Never True.” I collapse “Always” and “Often” into one category and “Sometimes” and “Never” into another category, then code each such that the work-family conflict experience is coded as “1.” I then sum the three dichotomized measures into a single scale (ranging from 0 to 3). In supplementary analyses, I test the use of alternative measurements, including a work-life conflict index with the Likert work-family conflict variables (ranging from 3–12), and the results are fully robust.

#### Controls.

To account for potential confounding variables in the relationship between schedule instability and respect, I use several demographic and work-related controls, including age, racial/ethnic background, education, English as a second language, marital status, parental status, involuntary part-time status, and job tenure. I also include other measures of job quality beyond schedule instability, such as respondents’ hourly wages and the benefits available to workers from their job. For benefits, I include dichotomous measures of whether workers received various benefits in their job (paid sick leave, paid family leave, paid vacation, health insurance, dental insurance, retirement plan, tuition assistance, and childcare). I also leverage the employer-employee linked data by including employer fixed effects, which allows me to net out unobserved, time-invariant firm characteristics that may shape workers’ experiences of respect and recognition.

### Analytical Approach

I begin by providing descriptive statistics on the sample and the distribution of both the dependent (supervisor respect and fair treatment) and independent (schedule instability) variables, including the distributions by gender. Next, I estimate OLS regression models that identify the association between the two dignity outcome variables (Y) and five measures of schedule instability (equation 1), where (S) is a vector of just-in-time scheduling practices, (D) is a vector of demographic controls, (W) is a vector of job-related characteristics, and (γf) is a firm fixed effect. (1) Y i = β 0 + β 1 S i + β j D + β k W + γ f + ε i I then estimate a similar model, but replace the vector of scheduling practices with the schedule instability scale (SIS) (equation 2). (2) Y i = β 0 + β 1 S I S i + β j D + β k W + γ f + ε i I conduct two supplementary analyses shown in the online appendix. First, I conduct an analysis using “seemingly unrelated regression” (SUR) (Zellner 1962), which compares the coefficients between two models that contain the same independent variables but different dependent variables. Each of these equations is estimated separately, but SUR analysis assumes that individual error terms are correlated across equations, resulting in greater efficiency in estimating parameters. In this case, I compare the coefficients between the effect of the schedule instability scale on customer respect and a) supervisor respect and b) supervisor recognition.

Theoretically, there should be no significant relationship between schedule instability and customer respect, but we might worry that workers who receive poor schedules may also feel more disrespected from or treated unfairly by their supervisor for some other reason. Workers simultaneously experience (and the Shift Project measures) respect from customers, which should not have the same relationship with schedule instability as supervisor respect, but may have the same confounding process, insofar as any omitted variables that bias the estimates for supervisor respect and recognition would likely also bias the estimates for customer respect. Using SUR analysis essentially nets out the effect of unobserved worker or job characteristics on supervisor respect and recognition. Therefore, the difference in the coefficients across models represents, in one sense, the “true” effect of schedule instability on these dignity outcomes, as “customer respect” effectively captures the portion of the coefficient from omitted variable bias (OVB). I conduct a paired t-test to determine the significance of this difference between coefficients. I find significant differences for most schedule instability variables (schedule instability scale and four of five practices for perceived respect; schedule instability scale and two of five practices for perceived recognition, with two more that are marginally significant). This is a conservative test, offering lower-bound estimates of the effect of schedule instability on supervisor respect and recognition.

Second, there may be some concerns that some unobserved individual trait shapes respondents’ assessments of dignity in the workplace (e.g., a respondent may be a generally negative or cynical person who assesses relationships more critically). Following Roscigno, Yavorsky, and Quadlin (2021), I include a control for respondents’ background disposition (operationalized as general happiness) to address potential concerns around respondents’ assessments of dignity being driven by personal outlook. Respondents were asked, “Taken all together, how would you say things are these days? Would you say you are…” with response options of “Very Happy,” “Pretty Happy,” and “Not Too Happy.” Results are fully robust to this specification.

Next, I turn to investigating the potential moderating effect of gender on the relationship between perceived supervisor respect and recognition and schedule instability. I do so by including an interaction term between the schedule instability scale and gender.
